activities.anchor: only what a camera can see or a speaker can say
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the format briefing
activities.name: swFormatSpot

config.prompt: A note to a new spec-script writer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Spec scripts are written in Courier 12-point, present tense.
One page of screenplay roughly equals one minute of screen time.
Spec scripts carry detailed shot directions, since the writer is planning the camera work.
Lean action lines and generous white space are pace made visible.
Non-standard format reads as amateur before the story gets a chance.
config.correction: Spec scripts carry no shot directions — that vocabulary belongs to the shooting script.
config.why: Readers triage hundreds of scripts; a script is a machine for convincing busy people, and format is the first filter.

activities.anchor: a complete three-act structure in about three minutes
activities.caption: rebuild For the Birds, beat by beat
activities.name: swBirdsOrder

config.prompt: Pixar's wordless three-act short — put the beats in order:
items: Small birds on a wire — a status order established
A big, gangly bird lands mid-wire — the small ones crowd away
The want escalates: get him off
They peck his feet until he drops — turn one
The wire, relieved of his weight, recoils — turn two
Naked, featherless birds in the grass as one feather drifts down
config.why: One premise, one turn, no B-stories — the entire craft in miniature, staged shot by shot.

activities.anchor: the board forces three early decisions
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the storyboard's three decisions
activities.name: swBoardCloze

config.text: The digital workflow adds %%0%% — the boards cut together with scratch sound and timed, really a first edit you can watch before shooting a frame. The board forces three early decisions: %%1%% (who owns the frame and when), %%2%% (staging the 180-degree line before the shoot, not during), and coverage (whether the scene's turns are photographable at all).
config.hint: A storyboard is the screenplay's second draft in pictures.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the compressed feature
activities.name: swShortPredict

config.q: A writer treats a short film as a compressed feature, opening with a world-building first act. What happens?
choices: The short breathes — features and shorts reward the same patience
The worst of both: a premise too big for its runtime, a runtime too long for its premise
config.why: A short must open with its conflict already running and reach a turn inside minutes — one premise, one turn, no B-stories.

activities.caption: call the deadline — the reader's patience
activities.name: swTenPageEstimate

config.prompt: Development readers triage hard. If premise, voice and control have not appeared, by roughly what page does the script rarely get another chance?
config.why: The ten-page reality: without premise, voice and control by then, the script rarely gets page eleven.
config.context: The Black List (Franklin Leonard's annual survey, running since 2005) exists because verdicts are opinions with a track record — not measurements.

activities.anchor: for other people's scripts and your own
activities.caption: pair each criterion with its question
activities.name: swCriteriaMatch

config.prompt: Five defensible criteria — pair each with the question it asks:

pairs.right: can the premise be stated in two sentences with protagonist, goal and obstacle?
does each scene change a value — info, power, safety, intimacy?
is the external goal visibly different from the internal lesson?
cover the names — can you still tell who is speaking?
what does the ending actually argue, and did the climax earn it?

config.why: The beats are diagnostic instruments — they locate where a draft's energy sags, but they cannot create the thing they measure.

activities.anchor: the turns are positional rather than plot-shaped
activities.caption: template turn versus positional turn — drag between them
activities.name: swDinnerCompare

config.prompt: Two kinds of scene turn — drag the divider:

before.label: plot-shaped
before.text: What the template expects: events collide, a value flips, the scene ends changed. By that ruler, two men talking over dinner for an entire film should be killed on the page.

after.label: positional
after.text: What My Dinner with André does instead: Wally resists André's spiritual odyssey beat by beat, and the value at stake — how to live — shifts from defence to reflection to the taxi ride home, where the coffee cup is rediscovered with new eyes.

config.why: The criteria are real and the criteria have limits — a template would have passed on this film, and missed it.

activities.anchor: where most scripts are actually improved
activities.caption: the development meeting — trace the note
activities.name: swNotesBranch

config.root: You are in the development meeting. The reader across the table says: 'the second act drags.'

start.text: What do you do with the note?

choices.label: Go tighten the second act
choices.feedback: You treated the report, not the patient.

choices.label: Diagnose before editing — where does the want break down?
choices.feedback: The professional move: separate the note from the disease.

choices.label: Dismiss it — verdicts are just opinions
choices.feedback: Half right, which is the dangerous half.

symptom.text: The fix usually lives somewhere else entirely — a mis-chosen midpoint, or a protagonist without a want in Act One — and the second act still sags in the next draft.

diagnose.text: Run the classic failure modes: the passive protagonist (things happen to them until page ninety), the theme stated instead of dramatised, the antagonist who is only as smart as the plot requires.

dismiss.text: Verdicts are opinions with a track record, true — but good notes describe real experience ('I stopped worrying about her here'), and experience is data.

config.why: Good note-takers describe their experience rather than prescribe rewrites; good note-takers-on diagnose before editing.
